sources: NOAA National Ocean Service, What is the most venomous marine animal?: the Australian box jellyfish is considered the most venomous marine animal; tentacles covered in nematocysts, tiny darts loaded with poison; victims may experience paralysis, cardiac arrest and even death within a few minutes of being stung; of about 50 box jellyfish species only a few have venom that can be lethal to humans; Chironex fleckeri is the largest, body up to one foot across with tentacles up to 10 feet long; clusters of eyes on each side of the box; can swim at speeds approaching four knots; may actively hunt shrimp and small fish; lethal kinds found mainly in the Indo-Pacific and northern Australia; https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/box-jellyfish.html

Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology), Chironex fleckeri: as many as 15 tentacles from each of the four corners (pedalia), up to 3 m long; transparent bell; 24 eyes but no brain; symptoms include extreme pain, shortness of breath and purple welts; more than 60 deaths in the last 100 years; an antivenom can save lives if given quickly; box jellyfish nets have been built on beaches where stings occur; https://animaldiversity.org/site/accounts/information/Chironex_fleckeri.html

Bielecki et al. 2014, PLoS ONE 9(6): e98870: cubozoans rely on 24 special-purpose eyes, six on each of four rhopalia, two of them lens eyes comparable to vertebrate eyes; https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0098870

O'Reilly, Isbister, Lawrie, Treston & Currie 2001, Medical Journal of Australia 175(11): 652-655, Prospective study of jellyfish stings from tropical Australia, including the major box jellyfish Chironex fleckeri: 40 patients over 12 months at Royal Darwin Hospital, 28 typical of C. fleckeri; severe envenoming was rare, none life-threatening, no antivenom given, no deaths; https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2001/175/11/prospective-study-jellyfish-stings-tropical-australia-including-major-box

beats.say: You can barely see it in the water. But its tentacles can stop your heart in minutes.
Up to fifteen tentacles on every corner. Each one up to ten feet long.
The box jellyfish. Called the most venomous animal in the sea.
Its tentacles are covered in tiny darts, loaded with venom.
It has twenty four eyes. And no brain.
And unlike most jellyfish, it swims. Up to four knots.
Would Meatball survive? Probably. In one year of stings at a Darwin hospital, nobody died.
It lives in warm coastal water, in the Indo Pacific, and northern Australia.
Its see through bell can be about a foot across.
It hunts shrimp and small fish.
In that hospital study, there were forty stings. Not one was life threatening.
But a bad sting means extreme pain, trouble breathing, and purple welts.
Over the last hundred years, it's been blamed for more than sixty deaths.
Fast help matters. There is an antivenom.
Beaches where stings happen put up nets to keep them out.
And of about fifty kinds of box jellyfish, only a few can kill a person.
Would you swim there in stinger season?
